formation.title: The Reunification of Mongolia
formation.text:
The scattered tribes of the Mongolian steppe have been brought together once more. For generations since the collapse of the great empire, the heirs of Chinggis Khan have warred among themselves: Khalkha against Oirat, tumen against tumen, brother against brother. Now, at last, a single authority commands the loyalty of the steppe.

But what shall this new Mongolia become? The legacy of Chinggis Khan pulls in two directions. One path calls for the restoration of Chinggisid military authority: the iron discipline of the tumen, the decimal organization that once conquered half the known world. The other path, opened by contact with Tibetan lamas, promises a different transformation entirely: a Mongolia of monasteries and learning, where the khan's legitimacy flows not from the sword but from the dharma.

The choice will shape Mongolia's identity for generations to come.

This choice unlocks a destiny path in the Traditions tab.

options.text: Restore the tumens. We are the heirs of Chinggis Khan

modifiers.name: Chinggisid Restoration
modifiers.text: The great Khan has reunited the tumens under Chinggisid authority. Mongol riders sweep across the steppe once more, their iron discipline and nomadic resilience restored to the glory of old.

options.text: Embrace the Yellow Hat: the dharma shall guide our people

modifiers.name: Yellow Hat Patronage
modifiers.text: Mongolia has embraced the Gelug path, transforming from a confederation of warriors into a civilization of monasteries and learning. The bond between Khan and Lama brings stability, wisdom, and a new Mongolian identity.

advances.name: Steppe Horsemanship
advances.text: The Mongolian horse is small, hardy, and tireless. Mongol children learn to ride before they can walk, and every warrior maintains a string of remounts for campaign.

advances.name: Felt Ger Encampments
advances.text: The portable felt ger allows entire armies to carry their homes with them, maintaining supply lines across the vast steppe without fixed logistics.

advances.name: Horse Breeding Tradition
advances.text: Selective breeding of Mongolian horses produces mounts legendary for endurance, able to subsist on sparse steppe grass and cover enormous distances.

advances.name: Ovoo Veneration
advances.text: Sacred stone cairns mark the spiritual landscape of the steppe. Travelers pause to circle an ovoo three times and add a stone, honoring the spirits of sky, earth, and water.

advances.name: Wolf Hunt Drills
advances.text: The great winter wolf hunt serves as both training exercise and population control. Hunters form enormous circles that tighten over days: the same encirclement tactics used in war.

advances.name: Pastoral Wealth
advances.text: The five types of livestock (horses, cattle, sheep, goats, and camels) form the foundation of Mongolian wealth. Herds numbering in the thousands sustain the nation.

advances.name: Chinggisid Lineage
advances.text: Only a descendant of Chinggis Khan may rightfully rule the Mongols. This principle of blood legitimacy unites the steppe under recognized authority.

advances.name: Noyan Retinues
advances.text: Each noyan, a hereditary Mongol lord, maintains a personal retinue of heavily armored cavalrymen, the elite core around which the tumen's fighting strength is organized.

advances.name: Tumen Organization
advances.text: The decimal system organizes warriors into units of ten, hundred, thousand, and ten thousand. Each tumen operates as a self-contained army with its own command structure.

advances.name: Trans-Steppe Trade
advances.text: Merchants traverse the vast Mongolian steppe carrying furs, horses, and hides southward, returning with grain, silk, and iron goods from settled neighbors.

advances.name: Kurultai Tradition
advances.text: The great assembly of Mongol nobles convenes to elect khans, resolve disputes, and plan campaigns. This tradition of deliberative governance balances the khan's authority.

advances.name: Composite Bow Mastery
advances.text: Mongolian bowyers perfect the art of layering horn, wood, and sinew into compact recurve bows of extraordinary power, accurate from horseback at full gallop. The bowyers work where the herds give horn and sinew or the forest gives birch.

advances.name: Steppe Diplomacy
advances.text: Mongol diplomatic traditions blend threat and accommodation: the exchange of envoys, marriage alliances between noble houses, and the careful management of tribute relationships.

advances.name: Hide and Wool Processing
advances.text: Mongolian craftsmen transform raw animal products into valued trade goods: felt from wool, leather from hides, and furs that command premium prices in Chinese and Central Asian markets.

advances.name: Dayan Khan's Restoration
advances.text: Batumongke Dayan Khan reasserted Chinggisid central authority over the fractured Mongol confederation, distributing the six eastern tumens among his sons to create a new governing order.

event.title: Dayan Khan and the Six Tumens
event.text:
In the late fifteenth century, a child named Batumongke was proclaimed khan by the warrior-queen Mandukhai. Together they would reunite the fractured Mongol nation. Taking the reign name Dayan, 'the Great Yuan', he crushed the Oirat taishis and southwestern rebels, then reorganized the entire eastern Mongol confederation into six great tumens: the Chakhar, Khalkha, Uriankhai, Ordos, Tumed, and Yonshiyebu.

Each tumen was assigned to one of his eleven sons, creating a new aristocracy bound by blood to the Great Khan. This was no mere administrative reform: it was the rebirth of the decimal system that had once made Mongol armies invincible. For a generation, the steppe was united as it had not been since the time of Kublai Khan himself.

options.text: The six tumens ride as one

modifiers.name: Tumen Reorganization
modifiers.text: Dayan Khan's redistribution of the six eastern tumens among his sons restored order to a fragmented steppe, creating a military-administrative system that channels nomadic energy into organized strength.

advances.name: Yam Relay Posts
advances.text: The ortoo relay stations, spaced a day's ride apart across the steppe, allow messages and supplies to traverse Mongolia's vast distances with remarkable speed.

advances.name: The Six Tumens
advances.text: Dayan Khan's reorganization of the eastern Mongols into six great tumens (Chakhar, Khalkha, Uriankhai, Ordos, Tumed, and Yonshiyebu) restored the military-administrative framework of the empire.

advances.name: Mongolian Script
advances.text: The traditional Mongolian script, written in vertical columns, preserves chronicles, legal codes, and correspondence. Literacy spreads through scribal traditions maintained by noble households.

advances.name: Caravan Routes
advances.text: Trade routes crossing the Mongolian steppe connect China to Central Asia, carrying tea, silk, and porcelain eastward and furs, horses, and livestock westward.

advances.name: Steppe Fortification
advances.text: Watchtowers and defensive positions exploit the steppe's vastness. Scorched earth tactics and the hostile climate create attrition that breaks invading armies.

advances.name: Sky Worship Rites
advances.text: Tengri worship, veneration of the Eternal Blue Sky, binds the Mongolian identity to the limitless heavens above the steppe. Royal ceremonies invoke the sky's blessing on the khan's rule.

advances.name: Altan Khan's Reforms
advances.text: Altan Khan's 1578 alliance with the Dalai Lama initiated Mongolia's transformation from a shamanistic warrior culture to a Buddhist civilization, banning blood sacrifice and promoting monastic education.

event.title: The Meeting at Thegchen Chonkhor
event.text:
In 1578, Altan Khan of the Tumed invited Sonam Gyatso, head of the Gelug lineage of Tibetan Buddhism, to a great meeting on the steppe. The encounter would transform Mongolia forever. Altan Khan bestowed upon Sonam Gyatso the title 'Dalai Lama', Ocean of Wisdom, while the lama in turn recognized the khan as a reincarnation of Kublai Khan, the great patron of Buddhism.

Altan Khan decreed that shamanic blood sacrifices would cease, that the images of the ongon spirits would be destroyed, and that the Gelug dharma would become the faith of the Mongols. Within fifty years, tens of thousands of young Mongolian men had taken monastic vows. Erdene Zuu, the first great monastery, rose upon the ruins of ancient Karakorum.

But not all Mongols welcomed this transformation. Many clung to the old ways of Tengri worship, seeing the Yellow Hats as foreign interlopers who would sap Mongolian martial spirit. The tension between dharma and the eternal blue sky would define Mongolian identity for centuries.

options.text: Let the dharma illuminate the steppe

modifiers.name: Gelug Conversion
modifiers.text: The Yellow Hat teachings spread across the steppe. Monasteries rise where ovoos once stood alone, and the Mongolian script captures sutras alongside chronicles. A new era of learning and devotion transforms the face of the steppe.

options.text: The sky gods of our ancestors shall endure

modifiers.name: Eternal Blue Sky
modifiers.text: The ancient ways of Tengri endure. Shamans commune with the sky and earth, warriors draw strength from ancestral spirits, and the hostile steppe itself becomes Mongolia's greatest fortress.

advances.name: Keshig Tradition
advances.text: The keshig, the khan's personal guard, represents the finest warriors of Mongolia. Membership is a supreme honor, and keshig soldiers outrank ordinary commanders.

advances.name: Gelug Monasteries
advances.text: Great monasteries in the Gelug tradition rise across Mongolia. Erdene Zuu, built on the site of ancient Karakorum, houses a thousand monks and becomes the center of Mongolian Buddhist learning.

advances.name: Ming Border Markets
advances.text: The horse markets along the Ming-Mongol border exchange Mongolian warhorses and livestock for Chinese grain, tea, silk, and iron. This trade sustains the steppe economy.

advances.name: Imperial Guard Reform
advances.text: The keshig is reorganized along professional lines, with systematic training in both mounted and dismounted combat, creating an elite force loyal to the khan alone.

advances.name: Chinggisid Law Code
advances.text: Building on the legacy of the Great Yasa, Mongolian lawmakers codify steppe law into a comprehensive system governing inheritance, criminal justice, and the obligations of lords to their khan.

advances.name: Horse Relay Expansion
advances.text: The ortoo system is extended and strengthened. Fresh horses at every station allow riders to cover vast distances in days, binding the far-flung Mongolian territories together.

advances.name: Zanbuurch Corps
advances.text: Mongolian warriors adopt firearms from their Chinese and Central Asian neighbors. The zanbuurch, matchlock musketeers, bring gunpowder warfare to the steppe without abandoning mounted traditions.

advances.name: Khalka Unification
advances.text: The four Khalka khanates (Tushegtii, Setsen, Zasagt, and Jasaktu) acknowledge a common Mongolian identity, ending centuries of inter-Khalka rivalry.

event.title: Unity of the Khalka
event.text:
The Khalka Mongols, the largest and most central of the Mongol confederations, have at last achieved genuine unity. Where once the four Khalka khanates competed against each other and against the western Oirats, a common identity has emerged. Shared ancestry under the Chinggisid line, common pastures across the Mongolian heartland, and increasingly, a shared Buddhist faith have welded these disparate groups into a single nation.

This is no empire of conquest but something perhaps more durable: a people who recognize themselves as one. From the Altai Mountains to the Khingan Range, from the Gobi Desert to the Siberian forests, the Khalka identity becomes synonymous with Mongolia itself.

options.text: We are one people, one steppe

advances.name: Steppe Artillery
advances.text: Siege warfare comes to the steppe. Mongolian forces acquire and employ artillery pieces, adding a new dimension to a military tradition built on cavalry mobility.

advances.name: Jebtsundamba Lineage
advances.text: The Jebtsundamba Khutuktu becomes Mongolia's highest spiritual authority. Beginning with the brilliant Zanabazar, this line of incarnate lamas unites Buddhist piety with Chinggisid heritage.

event.title: The Jebtsundamba Khutuktu
event.text:
A remarkable figure has emerged to unite spiritual and temporal authority in Mongolia: the Jebtsundamba Khutuktu, recognized as the highest Buddhist incarnation on Mongolian soil. First established when Zanabazar, son of the Tushegtii Khan and a prodigy of art and theology, was identified as a reincarnation of the great scholar Taranatha, the institution of the Jebtsundamba would become the spiritual heart of Mongolia.

Zanabazar created the Soyombo script, designed magnificent Buddhist sculptures, and built monasteries that became centers of learning across the steppe. In his person, the ancient Chinggisid bloodline merged with Buddhist sanctity, creating a uniquely Mongolian form of Buddhist authority that commanded loyalty from warrior and monk alike.

options.text: The Living Buddha guides our people

advances.name: Nomadic Resilience
advances.text: Generations of steppe life have bred extraordinary endurance into the Mongolian soldier. They fight on minimal supplies, endure extremes of cold and heat, and recover from setbacks that would destroy settled armies.

advances.name: Border Defense System
advances.text: Mongolia establishes a coordinated defense network across its frontiers, combining mobile cavalry patrols, garrisoned watch posts, and the rapid communication of the ortoo relay system.

advances.name: Steppe Modernization
advances.text: New technologies and methods reach the steppe. Fixed settlements grow alongside the nomadic camps, and Mongolia begins to develop the infrastructure of a modern state.

advances.name: Mongolian Cultural Renaissance
advances.text: A flowering of Mongolian arts and letters: new chronicles record national history, Buddhist art achieves new heights of refinement, and the Soyombo script symbolizes a confident Mongolian identity.

advances.name: National Cavalry Reform
advances.text: Mongolia's legendary cavalry tradition is adapted to modern warfare. Mounted units integrate firearms and artillery support while preserving the mobility and horsemanship that defined Mongol armies for centuries.

advances.name: Legacy of the Eternal Blue Sky
advances.text: The ancient Tengri heritage (the reverence for sky, earth, and the spirits of nature) blends with Buddhist philosophy to create a uniquely Mongolian spiritual tradition that endures across the ages.

advances.name: Modern Administration
advances.text: Mongolia develops a centralized administrative system, replacing the informal authority of nomadic khans with systematic governance, record-keeping, and bureaucratic institutions.

advances.name: Great Steppe Legacy
advances.text: The martial traditions of the steppe live on. Mongolia's armies maintain the cavalry excellence and nomadic endurance that once conquered the largest contiguous empire in human history.

destiny.name: Destiny of Mongolia
destiny.text: Mongolia has been reformed. The steppe awaits a new purpose: will the heirs of Chinggis Khan reclaim their empire, or forge a new path entirely?

event.title: The Destiny of Mongolia
event.text:
Mongolia stands reformed, a power of the steppe once more. The great sky stretches endlessly overhead, and beneath it the Mongolian nation draws breath for the first time in generations. But what shall this nation become?

The path chosen at our formation now opens before us. Whether we march toward the restoration of the Great Yuan or toward a new era of dharma and learning, the destiny of the Mongolian people is ours to shape.

options.text: The Eternal Blue Sky watches over us

destiny.name: Return to Dadu
destiny.text: The old Yuan capital beckons. Seize Dadu, the summer capital at Shangdu and the northern gateway at Datong to announce that the Great Khan has returned.

conditions.text: Own Dàdū, or a subject owns it
Own Dàtóng, or a subject owns it
Own Shàngdū, or a subject owns it

event.title: Mongol Banners Over Dadu
event.text:
The great city of Dadu (Khanbaliq, the City of the Khan) has fallen to Mongolian arms once more. Not since Toghon Temur fled northward in 1368 has a Mongol ruler sat in the old Yuan capital. The Forbidden City that Kublai Khan built stands as it always has, waiting for its rightful masters.

With the summer capital at Shangdu retaken and Datong secured as the gateway between steppe and settled lands, the first step of the Great Yuan restoration is complete. The peoples of the north look to the Mongol banner with a mixture of awe and fear, for they remember what it meant the last time it flew over these walls.

options.text: Dadu is ours again, as it was always meant to be

destiny.name: The Mandate Reclaimed
destiny.text: Secure Manchuria and the Gansu corridor. With Shenyang and Lanzhou under Mongol control, the path to the heartland lies open.

conditions.text: Own Shěnyáng, or a subject owns it
Own Lánzhōu, or a subject owns it

event.title: The Northern Mandate
event.text:
With Manchuria under our heel and the Gansu corridor secured, the strategic position of the old Yuan dynasty has been restored in all but name. From Shenyang to Lanzhou, Mongol authority extends across the breadth of northern China.

But how shall we govern these vast conquests? Some counselors urge the path of terror: let the reputation of Mongol riders freeze our enemies in their tracks before battle is even joined. Others argue for disciplined occupation: the iron yoke of systematic Mongol administration that extracts tribute and soldiers from every conquered province.

options.text: Let the terror of our name go before us

modifiers.name: Terror of the Steppe
modifiers.text: The reputation of Mongol riders precedes them. Cities submit rather than face the consequences of resistance, and enemies hesitate to challenge the heirs of Chinggis Khan.

options.text: Discipline and order shall bind our conquests

modifiers.name: The Iron Yoke
modifiers.text: Systematic Mongol administration extracts soldiers and tribute from conquered provinces with ruthless efficiency, though the constant demand for troops wears on the people.

destiny.name: The Great Yuan Restored
destiny.text: Complete the restoration of Mongol supremacy. Hold the Central Plains, the southern capital, and command the Silk Road from Kashgar to Kaifeng.

conditions.text: Own Kāifēng, or a subject owns it
Own Hángzhōu, or a subject owns it
Own Kashgar, or a subject owns it

event.title: The Great Yuan Lives Again
event.text:
From the Silk Road cities of Kashgar to the canals of Hangzhou, from the Central Plains of Kaifeng to the steppe heartland of Karakorum, the Mongol empire has been reborn. What Chinggis Khan began and Kublai Khan perfected, we have now restored.

The question that faces every great conqueror now confronts us: shall we rule this empire from the Khanbaliq throne as emperors of a settled civilization, managing subjects and building institutions? Or shall we remain what we have always been: world conquerors, for whom the horizon is never the boundary but merely the next objective?

options.text: We shall rule from the Khanbaliq throne

modifiers.name: Throne of Khanbaliq
modifiers.text: The Great Khan rules from the Khanbaliq throne as emperor of a vast domain, commanding loyalty from diverse subjects and building the institutions of a settled empire.

options.text: The world itself is our birthright

modifiers.name: World Conqueror
modifiers.text: The Mongol drive for universal empire continues. Intelligence networks and legal pretexts for war are developed at pace, though maintaining such vast armies strains the treasury.

destiny.name: The Dharma Comes to the Steppe
destiny.text: Forge the spiritual bond between Mongolia and Tibet. Control Lhasa and accumulate the wealth to sustain a Buddhist civilization on the steppe.

conditions.text: Own Lhasa, or a subject owns it

event.title: The Light of the Dharma
event.text:
The sacred bond between Mongolia and Tibet has been sealed. With Lhasa under Mongolian protection, the Yellow Hat teachings flow freely northward across the mountains. Monks from Drepung and Sera travel to the steppe, founding monasteries and teaching the dharma to eager Mongolian students.

This is not merely a matter of faith. The monasteries bring literacy, record-keeping, medicine, and a cosmopolitan network of learning that connects Mongolia to the wider Buddhist world. The wealth accumulated through careful stewardship sustains this transformation, proving that Mongolia can be great without conquest alone.

destiny.name: The Sangha Realm
destiny.text: Build a prosperous Buddhist kingdom through trade and learning. Fill the treasury, secure tea in your markets, and let wisdom replace the sword.

conditions.text: A market the country is in

children.text: Tea is produced in the market
Tea is traded in the market

event.title: A Kingdom of Monks and Merchants
event.text:
Mongolia has become something its warrior ancestors would scarcely recognize: a prosperous realm of monasteries, markets, and learning. The monasteries lend out their herds and their silver and manage a growing wealth of their own, while the tea trade with China enriches every settlement along the caravan routes.

But which aspect of this transformation shall we emphasize? Some advocate deepening the monastic tradition: building more monasteries, training more scholars, letting the wisdom of the sangha guide our nation's growth. Others point to the tea road and argue that Mongolia's future lies in trade: that the wealth flowing through our markets will accomplish what armies never could.

options.text: Deepen the wisdom of the sangha

modifiers.name: Monastic Wisdom
modifiers.text: The monasteries have become the engines of Mongolian growth, attracting settlers and merchants. But prosperity can breed complacency in a nation that once lived by the sword.

options.text: The tea road is our path to greatness

modifiers.name: Tea Road Riches
modifiers.text: The great tea caravans crossing the steppe pour wealth into Mongolian coffers and open diplomatic channels, though the influx of silver drives prices upward.

destiny.name: The Eternal Dharma
destiny.text: Transform Mongolia into an enduring center of Buddhist civilization. Raise Karakorum again around the monastery of Erdene Zuu, and give it a library where the scriptures are kept and turned into Mongolian.

conditions.text: We own Karakorum and it has a Library
We own Karakorum and its development is at least 6

event.title: The Eternal Dharma of the Steppe
event.text:
Mongolia has achieved what no one thought possible: a nomadic civilization that rivals any settled kingdom in learning, prosperity, and culture. The great monastery complex at Erdene Zuu stands on the ruins of ancient Karakorum, where once the world's conquerors held court. Now it is monks and scholars who gather here, not warriors.

The Soyombo script created by Zanabazar has become a symbol of Mongolian identity itself, adorning everything from monastery gates to official documents. Shall we carry Zanabazar's vision forward: using culture and art as the tools of soft power? Or shall we build a universal sangha, a Buddhist community that transcends borders and binds all peoples of the steppe under the dharma's gentle authority?

options.text: Zanabazar's vision shall be our guide

modifiers.name: Soyombo Legacy
modifiers.text: Zanabazar's cultural achievements (the Soyombo script, Buddhist sculpture, and monastic architecture) become tools of Mongolian soft power, winning influence where armies cannot.

options.text: Let the sangha unite all peoples

modifiers.name: Universal Sangha
modifiers.text: The Buddhist sangha transcends borders, creating a spiritual community that eases relations with fellow Buddhist nations and gives the clergy unprecedented influence.

units.name: Khorchin Raider
units.text: Light cavalry from the eastern Khorchin tribes, famed for their speed and raiding prowess. They strike like the steppe wind: swift, sudden, and gone before the enemy can respond.

units.name: Noyan Heavy Cavalry
units.text: The armored retinue of a Mongol lord, clad in lamellar armor and wielding lance and saber. They form the shock force that breaks enemy formations.

units.name: Mangudai
units.text: Elite mounted archers who specialize in feigned retreat tactics, drawing enemies into pursuit before wheeling to deliver devastating volleys. Their name means 'brave ones of fortune.'

units.name: Tumen Cavalry
units.text: The disciplined core of the Mongolian army, organized in the ancient decimal system. Tumen cavalry combine the mobility of steppe horsemen with the coordinated discipline of professional soldiers.

units.name: Keshig Guard
units.text: The khan's personal guard, chosen from the finest warriors of every tumen. Keshig soldiers are the most trusted and skilled fighters in Mongolia, sworn to defend the khan with their lives.

units.name: Zanbuurch Musketeers
units.text: Mongolian warriors armed with matchlock firearms adopted from Chinese and Central Asian neighbors. They combine the accuracy of settled musketeers with the toughness of steppe fighters.

units.name: Khalkha Hussars
units.text: Reformed Mongolian cavalry equipped with carbines and sabers, blending centuries of steppe horsemanship with modern military discipline and firearm tactics.

buildings.name: Ger Encampment
buildings.text: A semi-permanent camp of portable felt tents that serves as a military staging ground. The ger encampment provides shelter, storage, and a rallying point for levy forces.

buildings.name: Bowyers' Camp
buildings.text: A camp of bowyers beside the herds or at the forest's edge. A bow is a year in the making: a birch core, horn on the belly, sinew on the back, all bound with fish glue and left to cure.

children.text: The location's raw material is Livestock
The location's raw material is Lumber

buildings.name: Ortoo Relay Station
buildings.text: A station in the yam postal relay system, maintaining fresh horses and riders to carry messages and supplies across the vast Mongolian steppe with extraordinary speed.

buildings.name: Ovoo Cairn
buildings.text: A sacred stone cairn where travelers pause to honor the spirits of sky, earth, and water. Ovoos mark holy places across the steppe and serve as gathering points for seasonal ceremonies.

buildings.name: Horse Breeding Grounds
buildings.text: Dedicated pastures where Mongolian horses are selectively bred for the endurance, hardiness, and speed that make them the finest warhorses of the steppe.

where.text: Horses is produced in the location's market
The location's raw material is Livestock

buildings.name: Kurultai Grounds
buildings.text: The great assembly ground where Mongol nobles gather to elect khans, declare wars, and resolve disputes. The kurultai tradition embodies the deliberative governance of the steppe.

buildings.name: Steppe Trading Post
buildings.text: A market settlement along the trans-steppe trade routes where Mongolian herders exchange livestock, furs, and hides for manufactured goods, grain, and luxury items from settled neighbors.

buildings.name: Scribal Workshop
buildings.text: A center for Mongolian calligraphy and record-keeping, where scribes copy chronicles, legal codes, and diplomatic correspondence in the elegant vertical Mongolian script.

buildings.name: Steppe Watchtower
buildings.text: A defensive lookout position on the open steppe, manned by garrison troops who can spot approaching enemies across vast distances and relay warnings through the ortoo system.

buildings.name: Gelug Monastery
buildings.text: A grand Buddhist monastery in the Tibetan Gelug tradition. Hundreds of monks study sutras, produce art, and maintain libraries that make these institutions the intellectual heart of Mongolia.

buildings.name: Border Market
buildings.text: A bustling market at the frontier where Mongolian horses, livestock, and furs are exchanged for Chinese grain, tea, silk, and manufactured goods. These markets sustain the steppe economy.

buildings.name: Incarnation Palace
buildings.text: The grand residence of the Jebtsundamba Khutuktu, Mongolia's highest incarnate lama. Part monastery, part royal court, it serves as the spiritual and cultural center of Mongolian Buddhism.

buildings.name: Felt Manufactory
buildings.text: An industrial-scale facility for processing Mongolian wool into high-quality felt, the essential material of steppe life used in everything from ger walls to saddle padding.

buildings.name: Yuan Imperial Palace
buildings.text: The restored palace of the Great Khan in Khanbaliq, rebuilt in the grandeur of the Yuan dynasty. From its halls, the Mongol emperor commands the wealth of China and the loyalty of a hundred peoples.

buildings.name: Erdene Zuu Complex
buildings.text: The great monastery complex at the site of ancient Karakorum, housing hundreds of monks, libraries of sacred texts, and workshops for Buddhist art. The spiritual heart of Mongolian civilization.

list.name: Khalkha Tüsheet Confederation
list.text: After Dayan Khan's reunification (c.1500-1517) the Khalkha realm crystallised into three Chinggisid khanates: Tüsheet (centre), Sain Noyon (west, separated 1725), and Zasagt (far west). The three khans sat together at the Khüree Chuulgan to decide war, succession, and tribute, a structural compromise between universal-khan claims and the Borjigin princes' patrimonial autonomy. While maintained, the chuulgan meets and the federated levies turn out under one banner; while neglected, the three princely lines drift apart and the centre's writ runs only in its own otogs.

list.name: Bogd Gegen Lineage
list.text: In 1639 the Khalkha princes recognised the four-year-old Zanabazar (son of Tüsheet Khan Gombodorj and great-grandson of Abadai Khan) as the first Jebtsundamba Khutuktu, the supreme reincarnated lama of Khalkha Mongolia. Trained in Tibet by the Fifth Dalai Lama, he refounded Erdene Zuu and the moving monastic capital of Ikh Khüree (later Urga). The lineage combined a Chinggisid bloodline with a Gelug reincarnation, producing a sacred office whose legitimacy outlived any temporal khan. Available only when the realm has embraced Tibetan Buddhism.

list.name: Khalkha Jirum
list.text: Compiled between c.1709 and 1770 by the Khalkha grand assembly under the Tüsheet Khan and the second Jebtsundamba Khutuktu. Its twenty-five chapters integrated Chinggis Khan's Yassa, Altan Khan's 1577 Buddhist edicts, the Oirat-Khalkha Ikh Tsaaz of 1640, and the Manchu-imposed Mongol-Oirat regulations. Cases were tried before panels of zaisangs (clan judges) under written articles, bypassing the patrimonial seigneurial courts. The standing code of Mongolia until the Manchu codifications of the 1780s superseded it.

list.name: Otog-Khoshuu Banner Administration
list.text: The post-Yuan Mongol commoners were organised into otogs (decimal-pastoral kin units of nominally a thousand households), each headed by an appointed taishi. Dayan Khan's settlement bound the otogs to the six tümens; the Khalkha princely lines turned them into hereditary khoshuus tied to a single noyan's household register, with their own pasture rotations, postal duty (örtöö), and muster lists. Transfer between khoshuus was forbidden and the noyan's word governed every commoner's movement. The Manchu Lifan Yuan inherited the system intact in 1691.

list.name: Yellow Hat Sangha Patronage
list.text: In 1578 Altan Khan of the Tümed met Sonam Gyatso at Yanghua Monastery; Altan bestowed the title Dalai Lama on Sonam Gyatso, who in turn proclaimed Altan a reincarnation of Khubilai Khan. The compact made the Mongol khans the temporal patrons of the Gelug order. Renewed by Abadai Khan's 1585 founding of Erdene Zuu on the ruins of Karakorum, and by Güshi Khan's 1642 conquest of Tibet on the Fifth Dalai Lama's behalf, the patronage granted monasteries shabinar (lay servant-households) exempt from princely taxation: a fiscal privilege that drained the noyans and built Mongolia's monastic economy. Available only when the realm has embraced Tibetan Buddhism.
